https://www.rollingstone.com/culture/cul.text: By Daniel Kreps Daniel Kreps Contact Daniel Kreps on X Contact Daniel Kreps by Email View all posts by Daniel Kreps July 19, 2026 Tristan and Andrew Tate Andrei Pungovschi/Getty Images Andrew and Tristan Tate were arrested in Miami Saturday as British authorities sought their extradition on new charges of rape, sex trafficking, and “offenses relating to indecent images of a child.” The sibling social media influencers were taken into custody by the U.S. Marshals on a sealed warrant that the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) revealed Sunday morning. “We have decided to prosecute Andrew and Tristan Tate for further offenses including rape, arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation and offenses relating to indecent images of a child,” Malcolm McHaffie, Head of the Special Crime Division at the Crown Prosecution Service, said in a statement. “These charging decisions followed receipt of a further file of evidence from Bedfordshire Police and bring the total number of alleged victims in this case to seven. The CPS has requested the extradition of the Tates from the US. They have been arrested and await extradition proceedings to the UK.” In May 2025, the CPS charged Andrew and Tristan Tate with 11 and 10 counts respectively — including three each for rape — based on accusations from three victims in the U.K. The additional charges stem from allegations from a fourth victim. “The CPS has decided to prosecute Andrew Tate , 39, with seven further counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, three counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and 19 additional charges for offenses relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography,” the CPS said Sunday of the additional charges. “The CPS has decided to prosecute Tristan Tate, 38, with one count of sexual assault, two counts of rape and three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation.” In total, the brothers now face 59 charges combined. The Tate brothers’ lawyer Joseph McBride denied the allegations in a statement to the Associated Press and accused the U.K. of “filth and slander” in response to a defamation lawsuit the brothers filed against the U.K. government. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century “They’re pulling out all the stops to make sure these guys never get their day in court,” McBride said. “We are confident that once a competent judge sees the facts, and once the Department of Justice confronts this egregious abuse of its own authority, Andrew and Tristan Tate will walk free. America does not do Britain’s political dirty work.” Trending Stories 50 Years Ago Today: An Exhausted Elvis Presley Plays a Lackluster Matinee in Virginia Selena Gomez, Becky G, and Benny Blanco Just Dropped the Video of the Summer Phil Collins Reveals He Nearly Died in 2024 Amid Battle With Alcohol Addiction The Michigan Senate Primary Is a Battle for Democrats’ Future The Tate brothers, who hold dual citizenship in the U.S. and U.K., were previously charged with sex trafficking in Romania and were also under criminal investigation in Florida. In February, the brothers were authorized to leave Romania and return to the U.S. Last July, a court ruled that the pair could leave Romania, but not the European Union . In December, a judge said the case could not go to trial because of various legal and procedural irregularities tied to the prosecution. This required investigators and prosecutors to bring forward new evidence to bolster their charges, or amend the indictment. The investigation in Romania remains open. Beállítom Brüsszel legdrágább negyedében vásárolt volna újabb értékes ingatlant az Orbán-kormány. A magyar EU-elnökség épülete melletti ingatlanban a magyar gasztronómiát népszerűsítő luxuséttermet is nyitottak volna, a beruházásra pedig 7,2 milliárd forintot különítettek el – derült ki a HVG birtokába került nem nyilvános kormányhatározatból. A kormányhatározat nem sokkal a kormányváltás előtt született, a Magyar Közlönyben azonban nem jelent meg. A lap szerint az ingatlan egy részében fine dining étterem működött volna, a többi részét diplomáciai és protokollcélokra szánták. A Parc de Bruxelles-en lévő ház gyakorlati haszna viszont azért is kérdéses, mert a mellette lévő, korábban vásárolt hatalmas Magyarország Ház sincs megfelelően kihasználva. Végül az ingatlanvásárlás nem valósult meg, a HVG-vel a Magyar Nemzeti Vagyonkezelő Zrt. azt közölte: az adásvételi szerződést nem írták alá a felek. A lap úgy értesült, annak, hogy a vásárlás meghiúsult, nem a Fidesz választási veresége és a kormányváltás volt az oka, hanem a „kereskedelmi tevékenység célú funkcióváltásra” szóló engedély megszerzése. Emellett a tulajdonos által vállalt teljes körű felújítás műszaki tartalma sem felelt meg az elvárásoknak. Az előző kormányhoz és a Fideszhez köthető brüsszeli ingatlanvásárlásokról ebben a cikkünkben írtunk bővebben, itt pedig a Magyarország Házról és arról, hogyan lett a közpénzen vett ingatlan – egy forrásunk megfogalmazásában – „patrióta klubhelyiség”, ahol többször a Fidesz európai pártcsaládjának programjait tartották. https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.text: People look toward the downtown skyline from the Toronto Islands as forest fires cause poor air quality over the city. Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen People look toward the downtown skyline from the Toronto Islands as forest fires cause poor air quality over the city. Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty Images The Saturday read Wildfires ‘I couldn’t breathe’: the deadly health burden of wildfire smoke Scientists race to untangle complex links between exposure and mortality as fire weather grows more prevalent Ajit Niranjan Sat 8 Aug 2026 01.00 EDT Share A thousand kilometres from the infernos gorging on northern Ontario’s boreal forests, Erin O’Connor watched the sky above Canada’s biggest city turn an “almost post-apocalyptic” orange as it filled with light-scattering particles of soot and ash. Stepping outside the halls of Toronto General hospital, where air filters were keeping patients safe from the worst of the fumes, she was struck by a smell so strong it felt like standing by a campfire. “It really hit you in the face as soon as you walked outside,” said O’Connor, who runs University Health Network’s emergency department and saw a rise in patients presenting with allergies and shortness of breath. “As the days progressed, it was like that everywhere. It seemed even inside you could smell that burning.” Far more than the flames that have engulfed southern Europe and North America in recent weeks, it is the smoke that dominates the astonishing death toll from combusting nature. Thick with toxic gases that inflame the airways and tiny particulates that breach the lungs and ride the bloodstream to hit every organ in the body, fumes from landscape fires kill 1.5 million people each year, a study in the Lancet found in 2024 – more than floods, flames, storms and heat combined. So damaging are the lung-scarring effects of charred plant matter that people far from the fires may still perish. The plumes spewed by wildfires in Canada in 2023 caused 82,000 early deaths, a study in Nature found last year, with unfavourable winds pushing a third of the mortality burden into the US and another quarter into Europe. About 10% of the UK’s fine particulate pollution (PM2.5) comes from biomass burned abroad, researchers found in March. View image in fullscreen The Quilpituk Creek wildfire in British Columbia, seen here across Okanagan Lake. Photograph: Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press/AP Yet while scientists agree the health burden of wildfire smoke is jaw droppingly large, they are only beginning to untangle the complex links between exposure and mortality. The open research questions are growing more pressing as climate breakdown makes fire weather more severe. What if hotter infernos cause pollution to peak at even more extreme levels? What if bad air lasts several days or weeks? What if a severe episode hits before a person has fully recovered from the last bout of smoke? Whims of the wind The lack of answers in the existing research makes it hard to get a handle on how brutal the fallout from this furious fire season will be. Early signs are troubling, with vast tracts of vegetation torched close to big European cities and, after a late but explosive start to the North American fire season, smoke choking major population centres such as Chicago and New York City. In Toronto, which briefly had the worst air quality of any major metropolis in the world last month – a title claimed by Portland in the US on Wednesday – O’Connor said she could not remember the pollution ever having been so bad, with such a sudden onset that took so long to clear up. “I had never looked outside and had the sky seem orange in the middle of the day,” said O’Connor, who amid treating patients and fielding media requests rushed to pull her son from summer camp. “Certainly, we have had other wildfire smoke, but in more of a transient way.” Perhaps surprisingly, the death toll from a fire season can depend on the whims of the wind as much as the size of the fire. Wildfires in France spewed record amounts of pollution in the first half of the year and in Spain emissions have so far fallen just shy of the worst it has known. But even though monster infernos were halted alarmingly close to Madrid and Bordeaux , the smoke was mostly blown away from where people live. Daily particulate pollution levels still worsened across southern Europe and peaked at a staggering 342 micrograms of PM2.5 per cubic metre (μg/m³) in Bordeaux on 24 July – and 486 μg/m³ in Limoges, 180km (112 miles) away, the following day – but other big cities in southern Europe were spared the extremes that doctors fear. View image in fullscreen Wildfires across France, such as this one near Carcassonne, have been burning for weeks. Photograph: Pablo Cozzaglio/AFP/Getty Images North America has not been so lucky. As winds blew south and south-east from scarcely populated forests in Ontario and the Northwest Territories, at least 36 million people across the continent were breathing air fouled by “very unhealthy” concentrations of PM2.5 that exceeded 125.5μg/m³ on 16 July, preliminary analysis conducted for the Guardian shows. At least 10 million people were exposed to more than 250μg/m³, according to the estimates, a level of daily pollution that smog-choked New Delhi saw no more than eight times last year. Scientists say the hit to air quality in some big cities is reminiscent of the megafires in 2023 that came with vast death tolls. “As soon as we have massive population centres exposed, we’re going to see those increases,” said Stephanie Cleland, a wildfire health scientist at Simon Fraser University, who considered only people living within 25km of a measuring station in her calculations for the Guardian and said the figures are therefore conservative. “I would be concerned by the fact that it’s only been three years since this last happened and now we’re having it again.” ‘It felt like working in a war zone’ In a quiet suburb of Duluth, in north-east Minnesota, the worst of the smoke was seen, smelled and tasted on 16 July. Jae Jeon and Dan McClelland, a married couple who grow flowers for weddings and subscription deliveries, were looking forward to opening the windows after days baking in oppressive heat. Instead, they woke up to a fog that they soon realised was made up of something much worse. By late morning, their local hardware store had sold out of masks and air purifiers. People resorted to attaching furnace filters to box fans instead. The McClellands were among 12,000 people in west Duluth exposed to an average of 541μg/m³ of fine particulate pollution, the analysis shows, higher than anywhere else in North America. They sent their sole farmworker home early after she complained of a headache but, with two weddings coming up on the weekend and little chance of cancellation, they still had plenty of flowers to pick and arrange. The couple got to work harvesting roses, yarrows, clematises and sweet peas, surrounded by a dystopian haze the likes of which they had never experienced. “It felt like working in a war zone,” said Jae Jeon. “When I went outside, I couldn’t breathe, so I had to wear a mask, but it was still painful. After just a couple of minutes you started to get a headache.” View image in fullscreen People look out at the smog caused by wildfire smoke from the CN Tower in Ontario last month. yellowish-grey in Canada’s largest city. Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty Images Climate breakdown made last month’s fire weather twice as likely in Canada and France, and 20 times more likely in Spain, recent rapid analyses have found, the result of planet-heating emissions that have made it easier for vegetation to dry out. As plants and trees combust, they spew a host of harmful particles that also trigger damaging inflammatory responses as the body seeks to purge foreign objects. Scientists have relied on general air pollution relations to model the smoke’s chronic health effects, which make up the bulk of the death toll, because they lack long-term studies specific to wildfires. “The reason we don’t have them for wildfire smoke is because we haven’t had to deal with this as kind of a repeated ongoing problem,” said Michael Brauer, a wildfire health scientist at the University of British Columbia and co-author of the study on Canada’s 2023 fires . He first experienced wildfire smoke when he was about 40 years old, he said, while a 10-year-old child where he lives in British Columbia would have breathed it every summer of their life. Compounding climate events But the analogy to regular pollution is imperfect. Compared with other sources of PM2.5, such as factories or cars, wildfire smoke contains a greater share of organic compounds that increase inflammation and a higher concentration of ultra-fine particles that penetrate the deepest recesses of the lungs. PM2.5 from wildfire smoke is up to 10 times more harmful in the short-term, a study in Nature Communications found in 2021, and factoring this into epidemiological models suggests death tolls from short-term exposure to wildfire smoke have been greatly underestimated, a study in the Lancet Planetary Health found last year. Some researchers suggest high peak exposure during serious smoke episodes better explains why wildfire particulates do more damage than regular ones. “It may be that it’s because the smoke is chemically more toxic, or it may be – what I think is more likely – that it’s basically overwhelming your defences,” said Brauer, who compared it to having one drink a day for a year rather than bingeing 365 in 24 hours. “That’s clearly going to have different impacts.” When wildfire smoke gets bad, experts recommend wearing masks, closing windows and checking in on vulnerable neighbours, particularly old people with chronic disease who live alone. They also recommend checking air quality monitors in the morning and moving activities indoors when the pollution is too high. In some cases, actions to keep the air clean may conflict with efforts to stay cool, according to a report from the BC Lung Foundation published last month. “The issue is we have a lot of compound climate exposure events where you have heat and wildfire,” said Cathryn Tonne, an environmental epidemiologist at the Barcelona Institute for Global Health and co-author of the study modelling wildfire-specific PM2.5. “Being home with the windows closed can be very bad – if you don’t have air conditioning – if it’s also hot.” Can the fires behind the smoke at least be prevented? At the Fifa World Cup final, which barely avoided disruption from bad air, the US president, Donald Trump, asked his Canadian counterpart , Mark Carney, to “stop these fires from coming in and poisoning our air”. The demand was accompanied by threats of sanctions and came as Republican senators blamed Canada’s fires on poor forest management. Scientists countered that the blazes had little to do with land management – most of what has burned is boreal forest in unpopulated areas – and a lot to do with the rise in temperatures caused by burning fossil fuels, which Republicans have expanded. View image in fullscreen A view of Manhattan, New York from Brooklyn Bridge park as wildfire smoke from Canada causes smoggy conditions last month. Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty Images In Europe , though, changes in land use have alarmed firefighters and wildfire experts about as much as global heating. Rural regions across the Mediterranean have hollowed out, resulting in more overgrown vegetation that dries out and allows fires to spread more easily during the hotter heatwaves that climate breakdown has brought. The combination of the two factors has led Spanish wildfire scientists to warn that we have “entered an era of fires we cannot extinguish”. It is a problem that other parts of the world, from the western US to Australia, already know well. Adding to the climatic burden in the coming months is the arrival of a strong El Niño , a cyclical warming weather pattern, along with a related natural phenomenon in the Indian Ocean, which is priming countries across south-east Asia to burn. The McClellands said that – even though they still had their homes and their health – the episode had given them a taste of the suffering that climate breakdown has long caused in other countries. “I know that people all around the world are feeling a kind of helplessness because of climate disasters,” said Dan McClelland. “I feel like this opened my eyes to understand just a sliver of what other people are feeling.” Explore more on these topics Wildfires The Saturday read Canada France Americas Europe Climate crisis Extreme heat Share Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Gabriela Passos/AP Donald Trump Jr Democrat sends letter to White House over Trump Jr wedding bankrolled by Russian oligarch Robert Garcia expresses concern over ‘any possible foreign entanglement’ between White House and Umar Kremlev Ariana Baio Tue 15 Sep 2026 10.29 EDT Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 10.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, is investigating potential ties between the White House and a Russian oligarch who paid for a portion of Donald Trump Jr’s wedding. In a letter sent to Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, on Monday, Garcia expressed concern about “any possible foreign entanglement” between the president’s son and the oligarch, Umar Kremlev . Garcia asked Wiles to provide documents, records and communications between the White House and Trump Jr about Kremlev, among other requests. “As the son of President Donald Trump and the part-owner and major investor of multiple companies with extensive Department of Defense contracts, any apparent ties to members of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s inner circle raises serious questions about pay-to-play schemes and foreign intelligence infiltration of the President’s family,” Garcia wrote in the letter. Who is Umar Kremlev, the Russian oligarch who reportedly helped pay for Donald Trump Jr’s wedding? Read more In a separate letter addressed to Trump Jr, Garcia expressed similar worries and asked the president’s son to provide more details about his wedding events bankrolled by Kremlev, including: all dates of communication between Trump Jr and Kremlev, any communications Trump Jr may have had with the White House about Kremlev, financial records of purchases made by foreign nationals and a complete list of wedding gifts from foreign nationals. It came just hours after ProPublica revealed that the Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on wedding celebrations for Trump Jr and his wife, Bettina, earlier this year. The couple also confirmed Kremlev’s financial involvement on Monday. “I have no idea who Umar is, never heard of him, and he didn’t pay for Don and Bettina’s wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day from the wedding. It was an ‘afterparty’ given in their honor. Not a big deal! I was not present at the party,” the US president said in a statement in response to the report. “Why did a Russian oligarch close to Putin fund Trump Jr.’s wedding in the Bahamas?” Garcia wrote on X after the ProPublica report was published. Garcia added: “Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the President’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers.” Axios was the first to report on Garcia’s letter. The investigation into Trump Jr’s wedding is part of the House Oversight Committee Democrats’ larger investigation into the ways the Trump family has allegedly enriched themselves since President Donald Trump took office last year. The Guardian reached out to Garcia’s office and the White House for further comment. https://www.freepressjournal.in/india/wh.text: Four Central European nations Poland, Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, collectively known as the Visegrád Group (V4) have thrown their support behind India’s long-standing demand for a permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council (UNSC), adding a fresh diplomatic push to New Delhi’s campaign for reforms in the global body.The endorsement was announced on September 21, 2026, during the first high-level V4-India foreign ministers’ meeting, held on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York.Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár, speaking on behalf of the group, said the four countries agreed that India, as a member of the Global South and an emerging power in the Indo-Pacific, should have a permanent place at the Security Council. “We all agree, as V4 countries, that India, as part of the Global South, an upcoming superpower in the Indo-Pacific region, must be at the table as a permanent member of the UN Security Council,” Blanár said.External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar described the meeting as a “new historic occasion”, marking a significant step in India’s engagement with the Central European bloc.What Does V4’s Support Mean For India?The V4 endorsement adds four more countries to the growing international support for India’s bid for permanent membership of the UNSC. While the backing does not immediately change the composition of the Council, it strengthens New Delhi’s diplomatic efforts to build a broader consensus around reforming the United Nations’ principal body responsible for international peace and security.The support is particularly notable because it comes from a group of Central European countries, expanding the geographical reach of India’s campaign beyond its established diplomatic partners.India has consistently argued that the current structure of the Security Council does not adequately reflect contemporary geopolitical and economic realities. With the global balance of power having changed considerably since the UN was established in 1945, New Delhi has called for reforms that would give emerging economies and developing countries a greater role in international decision-making.The V4’s statement also explicitly recognises India’s role as a major voice of the Global South and an emerging power in the Indo-Pacific, adding to the diplomatic recognition of its expanding international influence.Why Is India Seeking A Permanent Seat At The UNSC?The United Nations Security Council currently has 15 members, comprising five permanent members and 10 non-permanent members elected for two-year terms.The five permanent members China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States hold veto power over substantive Council decisions. India has served as a non-permanent member of the UNSC several times, most recently during the 2021-22 term. However, it has long sought permanent membership, arguing that the Council’s existing composition does not adequately represent the world’s population, economic realities and changing political landscape.New Delhi has also pointed to its contributions to UN peacekeeping and its growing role in international affairs as part of its case for a greater role in global governance.India is a member of the G4, alongside Brazil, Germany and Japan. The four countries mutually support one another’s bids for permanent membership and advocate reforms to make the Security Council more representative.India has also received support in principle for its bid from major powers, including France, the UK, the US and Russia. The V4’s collective endorsement adds another regional grouping to the countries backing its demand.How Difficult Is UNSC Reform?Despite the growing number of countries supporting reform, securing a permanent seat remains a complicated diplomatic challenge.Any expansion of the Security Council’s membership requires amendments to the UN Charter. Such amendments must be adopted by a two-thirds majority of the UN General Assembly and ratified by two-thirds of UN member states, including all five permanent members of the Security Council.This means that support from individual countries and regional blocs, while politically significant, does not automatically translate into permanent membership.The reform process has faced prolonged disagreements over the number of additional permanent seats, the question of veto powers and which countries should be included in an expanded Council.China’s position on India’s permanent membership is also an important factor in the broader negotiations, given that Beijing is a permanent member whose ratification would be required for a Charter amendment to take effect.The V4 endorsement, therefore, adds diplomatic weight to India’s campaign but does not resolve the institutional and political obstacles that have held up reform.Beyond The UNSC: What Else Did India And V4 Agree On?The foreign ministers’ meeting was not limited to India’s demand for permanent membership. Both sides also discussed expanding cooperation across several strategic and economic sectors.India and the V4 countries agreed to hold annual foreign ministers’ meetings and establish an annual business forum to strengthen engagement between their governments and business communities.The two sides also agreed to deepen cooperation in areas including defence, technology, innovation, research, education, space, connectivity and people-to-people exchanges.They further expressed support for working together to strengthen multilateralism.These commitments provide a framework for more regular political engagement and could open up additional avenues for Indian businesses, institutions and strategic partnerships in Central Europe.Why This Matters For India’s Global RoleThe V4’s endorsement carries significance on two fronts: India’s campaign for a more representative Security Council and its broader engagement with Europe.India Has Served 8 Terms On UNSC, So Why Is It Still Seeking A Permanent Seat? For New Delhi, support from Poland, Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic adds to the range of countries and regional groupings backing its demand for reform. It also reinforces India’s efforts to present the case for permanent membership as part of a wider push for more inclusive global governance.At the same time, the agreement to expand cooperation in defence, technology, trade, research and connectivity gives the relationship a practical dimension beyond multilateral diplomacy.The endorsement does not guarantee a permanent seat for India, nor does it indicate that the long-stalled reform process is close to a breakthrough. However, it gives New Delhi another platform to build support for its position while strengthening ties with four European partners.For India, the meeting represents an opportunity to advance its UNSC reform campaign while developing a broader and more structured partnership with Central Europe.
